items.stem: What is the correct role of an API key in API Gateway?

options.text: To identify a client for usage plans and throttling, not to authenticate it
options.rationale: Correct: API keys track and meter clients via usage plans; they are not an authentication mechanism.

options.text: To securely authenticate the caller's identity
options.rationale: API keys are not an authentication mechanism and must not be relied on for identity.

options.text: To encrypt the payload in transit
options.rationale: TLS handles transport encryption, not API keys.
API keys do not replace IAM-based authorization.

items.explanation: Correct: API keys track and meter clients via usage plans; they are not an authentication mechanism.

items.stem: Which deployment approach shifts a small percentage of traffic to a new version to limit blast radius?

options.text: A canary release on the stage
options.rationale: Correct: a canary release routes a small traffic percentage to the new deployment.
Deleting a stage removes it entirely rather than testing gradually.
Turning off logging does not control traffic.
Cache TTL is unrelated to gradual rollout.

items.explanation: Correct: a canary release routes a small traffic percentage to the new deployment.

items.stem: Which TWO mechanisms help protect and control access to an API Gateway endpoint? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A Cognito or Lambda authorizer on the method
options.rationale: Correct: authorizers validate the caller before the request reaches the integration.

options.text: A resource policy restricting source VPC or IP
options.rationale: Correct: resource policies constrain who can invoke the API.
Cache size affects performance, not access control.
The API name has no security effect.

items.explanation: Correct: authorizers and resource policies both control access; cache and naming do not.
